'''''Helosciadium nodiflorum'''''<ref>{{cite web | url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:842893-1 | title=Helosciadium nodiflorum (L.) W.D.J.Koch | Plants of the World Online | Kew Science }}</ref> (synonym: ''Apium nodiflorum''), '''fool's watercress''',<ref name=IUCN/> is a flowering plant found in ditches or streams, as well as fresh and brackish-water wetlands native to western Europe. It is not poisonous to humans but it could be easily confused with the allegedly poisonous [[Berula erecta|lesser water parsnip]].

==Description==
''Helosciadium nodiflorum'' is a low-growing or prostrate hairless perennial up to 1 m tall, with a thick, hollow, faintly ridged stem which, when lying down (procumbent) produces roots at the nodes. It has glossy [[pinnate]] leaves, each of which has 4-6 opposite pairs of toothed, oval to lanceolate leaflets that are slightly paler green on the undersides. There are ridges at the nodes of the leaflets which are often paler than the [[rhachis]] and look like rings. (Note, this is different from [[Berula erecta|lesser water-parsnip]], which has a ring on the petiole.) The [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] are hollow with a distinctive single groove on upper surface, and may be streaked with red/purple lines; they are laterally inflated towards the base and clasp the stem.<ref name=Rose>{{cite book |last1=Rose |first1=Francis |title=The Wild Flower Key |date=2006 |publisher=Frederick Warne |location=London|isbn=978-0-7232-5175-0}}</ref> The crushed leaves smell of carrot.

[[File:Helosciadium nodiflorum2.jpg|thumb|200px|Close up of umbel flowers.]]

==Taxonomy==
In 2010 a taxonomic revision demonstrated that the genus ''Apium'' was [[Polyphyly|polyphyletic]] and needed to be split into three genera. Five of the 7 European species of ''Apium'' were therefore moved to the genus ''Helosciadium'', as had first been proposed by [[Wilhelm Daniel Joseph Koch|Wilhelm Koch]] in 1824. ''Apium nodiflorum'' was among them, and is therefore now correctly called ''Helosciadium nodiflorum'' W.D.J. Koch.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ronse |first1=A. |last2=Popper |first2=Z.A. |last3=Preston |first3=J.C. |last4=Watson |first4=M.F. |title=Taxonomic revision of European Apium L. s.l.: Helosciadium W.D.J.Koch restored |journal=Plant Systematics and Evolution |date=2010 |volume=287 |issue=1–2 |pages=1–17 |doi=10.1007/s00606-010-0284-3|bibcode=2010PSyEv.287....1R |s2cid=21921727 }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Helosciadium nodiflorum'' is common throughout England, Wales and Ireland but much less so in Scotland.<ref>[https://www.ukwildflowers.com/Web_pages/apium_nodiflorum_fools_water_cress.htm Apium nodiflorum] Peter Llewellyn Wild Flowers of the British Isles, Accessed 2011</ref> It often grows with [[Nasturtium officinale|watercress]] in wet places. It blooms in July and August and is found in wet habitats including ditches, springs, fens and ponds.<ref>[http://www.wildflowersofireland.net/plant_detail.php?id_flower=393&Wildflower=Fool's-water-cress Fool's-water-cress] Wild flowers of Ireland. Accessed July 2011 Apium nodiflorum Fool's-water-cress]</ref><ref>[https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/index.php?q=plant/apium-nodiflorum Apium nodiflorum (Fool's-water-cress)]</ref> The species is also widely documented from brackish estuarine/salt marsh habitats.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://envirolink.govt.nz/assets/Envirolink/1624-HZLC127-Manawatu-Wanganui-Estuaries-Habitat-Mapping-Vulnerability-Assessment-and-Monitoring-Recommendations-Related-to-Issues-of-Eutrophication-and-Sedimentation.pdf |title= |website=envirolink.govt.nz |access-date=7 September 2021}}{{title missing|date=September 2022}}</ref>

==Uses==
Wild fool's watercress has been traditionally harvested and consumed in several Mediterranean countries, including Spain, Italy, Portugal and Morocco<ref>{{cite book |last1=de Cortes Sanchez-Mata |first1=Maria |last2=Tardio |first2=Javier |title=Mediterranean Wild Edible Plants: Ethnobotany and Food Composition Tables |date=13 April 2016 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-1-4939-3327-3}}</ref> The edible young leaves and tender shoots can be used raw in salads, boiled, or used as a condiment in soups and other dishes.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Parada |first1=M |last2=Carrió |first2=E |last3=Vallès |first3=J |title=Ethnobotany of food plants in the Alt Empordà region (Catalonia, Iberian Peninsula) |journal=Journal of Applied Botany and Food Quality |date=2011 |issue=84 |pages=11–25 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/277175415}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Guarrera |first1=P.M. |last2=Savo |first2=V |title=Wild food plants used in traditional vegetable mixtures in Italy |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |date=2016 |volume=185 |pages=202–234 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2016.02.050 |pmid=26944238 |bibcode=2016JEthn.185..202G |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378874116300940|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
